I have gathered substantial material from the approved sources. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes. I have reached the tool limits, so I will work from the pages I was able to access and note where I could not retrieve certain denominational or scholarly perspectives.

## Psalm 34 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Title / Superscription

**v. Title: "Of David, when he pretended to be insane before Abimelech, so that the king drove him away."**

The historical background is 1 Samuel 21:10–15. David fled from Saul to Gath, where he was recognised and feared for his life. He feigned madness — scrabbling on gates and letting spittle run down his beard — and King Achish (called "Abimelech" here, likely a dynastic title of Philistine kings, as "Pharaoh" was for Egypt) drove him away in contempt. The psalm was probably composed later in the cave of Adullam (1 Sam 22:1–2), where David's band of desperate followers gathered. The psalm is an acrostic: each verse begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet (except *waw* is omitted). The acrostic format was a device to aid memorisation.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-34-commentary , https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/34.htm

**Modern scholarship note:** Ellicott argues that the psalm's proverbial, "gnomic" style and Aramaic-influenced language suggest composition far later than David, and that the title "is of no historic value" — the compiler may have been prompted by word-associations between the psalm's vocabulary and the 1 Samuel account (e.g., Hebrew *ta'amû*, "taste" in v. 8, resembling *ta'amô*, "his behaviour" in 1 Sam 21:13). The historical "blunder" of the king's name (Abimelech for Achish) is noted.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/34.htm

---

### v. 1 — "I will bless the LORD at all times; His praise will always be on my lips."

David resolves to praise God in *every* circumstance — not just in deliverance but "at all times," including adversity. Spurgeon notes the fixed determination: "He is resolved and fixed, *I will*." Praise is not merely in the heart but "in my mouth" — vocal, public, not silent. Gill notes this covers both temporal and spiritual blessings: temporal mercies are renewed daily, and spiritual blessings are irreversible, so continual praise is always fitting.
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php , https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/34.htm , https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-34-commentary

### v. 2 — "My soul boasts in the LORD; let the oppressed hear and rejoice."

David's boast is not in his own cleverness (his escape involved deception), but in the LORD who delivered him. Spurgeon calls this "holy boasting" — boasting in God's attributes, covenant, and works, where one can never be convicted of vanity. "The humble shall hear" — David calls God's people "the humble," as if pride were a denial of God. Those who are lowly will be glad to hear how God blesses humility.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php

### v. 3 — "Magnify the LORD with me; let us exalt His name together."

David invites others into praise. "Magnify" does not mean to make God bigger (He cannot be made larger), but to enlarge Him in one's *perception*. Spurgeon: "Who can make God great but those who feel themselves to be little?" The verse expresses the instinct of the regenerate life toward *congregated, social worship*. The psalmist feels his own inadequacy to glorify God alone and stirs up others.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php

### v. 4 — "I sought the LORD, and He answered me; He delivered me from all my fears."

David now gives his personal testimony. "I sought" (*darash*) means earnestly turning to God in prayer, not merely looking for Him as though lost. The sequence is simple: David sought, God answered, God delivered. Spurgeon observes that David's prayer at Gath must have been "in a very confused manner" — even a "poor limping prayer" — yet God accepted it and brought deliverance. There is debate over whether David sinned by feigning madness; Poole notes "whether he sinned or not, is matter of dispute; but this is undoubted, that God's favour and his deliverance at that time was very remarkable." Morgan notes the incongruity between the deceit and the exalted praise.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-34-commentary , https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php

### v. 5 — "Those who look to Him are radiant with joy; their faces shall never be ashamed."

David moves from "I" to "They" — his experience is not unique. "Looked" implies faith; "radiant" suggests faces lit up with joy. Kidner notes the word for "radiant" also appears in Isaiah 60:5, describing a mother's face lighting up at the sight of children long lost. "Never ashamed" means God never forsakes the one who trusts. Spurgeon: "Never did a sore heart look in vain to the good Physician."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php

### v. 6 — "This poor man called out, and the LORD heard him; He saved him from all his troubles."

David returns to his own case. "This poor man" — David, humiliated and acting the madman. "Cried" — Spurgeon reflects: "A cry is short, and not sweet… brief, and bitter… the language of pain… has much meaning and no music." Yet the Lord heard. Prayer can clear troubles "as easily as the Lord made riddance of the frogs and flies of Egypt." Gill sees a possible typological reference to Christ, "who was poor in temporals, though rich, and Lord of all."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php , https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/34.htm

### v. 7 — "The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him, and he delivers them."

**The key interpretive debate on this verse** concerns the identity of "the angel of the LORD."

- **Christ / Pre-incarnate Word view (Spurgeon, Gill, Keil & Delitzsch, Hengstenberg, many older commentators):** The "angel of the LORD" is the uncreated Angel, the covenant Angel — the pre-incarnate Christ — at the head of the heavenly host. Spurgeon: "The covenant angel, the Lord Jesus, at the head of all the bands of heaven, surrounds with his army the dwellings of the saints." Gill similarly notes this as the "uncreated Angel, the Lord Jesus Christ." Keil & Delitzsch identify this as "none other than He who was the medium of Jahve's intercourse with the patriarchs, and who accompanied Israel to Canaan." Constable (StudyLight.org) calls this "undoubtedly a reference to the Lord Himself… specifically, the pre-incarnate Christ."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php , https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/34.htm , https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-34.html

- **Collective / angelic host view (Calvin, Hupfeld, some moderns):** Based on the verb "encamps round about," which suggests plurality, some take "angel" collectively as the host of ministering spirits. Calvin says the psalmist teaches that God defends His people "by the power and ministration of angels" and that "angels… are ever intent upon the preservation of our life." MacLaren argues for the singular reading but acknowledges the collective interpretation is common.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/34-7.html , https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/psalms-34.html

- **General divine protection view (Ellicott):** Ellicott sidesteps the difficulty of one angel encamping "round about" by saying "angel of the LORD" here is a general expression for "the Divine manifestation of protection." It need not refer to a specific angelic being but to God's protective presence.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/34.htm

- **Guardian angel support:** Guzik notes this is "one passage that gives support to the thought of a guardian angel for everyone, or perhaps at least for believers," though it does not prove the idea.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/

### v. 8 — "Taste and see that the LORD is good; blessed is the man who takes refuge in Him!"

David moves from testimony to invitation: experience God's goodness *personally*. "Taste and see" are sensory metaphors for faith — faith as a spiritual sense. Poole: "Taste, i.e. consider it seriously, and thoroughly, and affectionately; make trial of it." The order is important: tasting (experience) precedes seeing (understanding). Bernard of Clairvaux: *Nisi gustaveris, non videbis* ("Unless you taste, you will not see"). Both Hebrews 6:5 and 1 Peter 2:3 allude to this verse to describe the first venture into faith.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-34-commentary , https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/34-7.html

### v. 9 — "Fear the LORD, you His saints, for those who fear Him lack nothing."

"Fear" here is reverent, childlike awe — not terror. This fear is closely connected to trusting God and experiencing His goodness (v. 8). The promise "no want" (lack nothing) is not a promise of luxury but of necessary provision. Spurgeon: "He may not give luxuries, but the promise binds him to supply necessaries."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php

### v. 10 — "Young lions go lacking and hungry, but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing."

Even the strongest and most self-reliant (young lions) may suffer hunger, but those who depend on God will not lack "any good thing." VanGemeren notes the lions may be "a metaphor for those who are strong, oppressive, and evil." Poole adds an important qualifier: "sometimes He knows… that wants and crosses are more needful and useful to them than bread, and in such cases it is a greater mercy of God to deny them supplies than to grant them." Trapp: "Paul had nothing, and yet possessed all things."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/34.htm

---

### vv. 11–14 — The "Sermon" Section: Living in the Fear of the LORD

At v. 11 the psalm shifts from hymn to sermon. David addresses "children" — likely his band of followers at Adullam (those in debt, distress, and discontent; 1 Sam 22:2). Spurgeon notes the pastoral heart: "Though a warrior and a king, the psalmist was not ashamed to teach children."

**v. 11:** "Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the LORD." The fear of the LORD can be taught — it is not merely a feeling but involves specific, concrete actions (vv. 13–14).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/

**v. 12:** "Who is the man who delights in life, who desires to see good days?" This is quoted in 1 Peter 3:10–12. Under the Old Covenant, long life and blessing were promised for obedience (Exod 20:12). Under the New Covenant, blessing is received by faith in Christ.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/

**v. 13:** "Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from deceitful speech." The fear of God shows itself first in speech. Gill notes the tongue "is an instrument of much evil, an unruly member, and needs restraint." Spurgeon: "Men cannot spit forth poison without feeling some of the venom burning their own flesh."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/34.htm , https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php

**v. 14:** "Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it." Negative and positive: depart from evil *and* do good. Peace is to be actively chased — "pursue it." Spurgeon: "Follow after peace when it shuns you." This was remarkable teaching for a band of rough, distressed men who would naturally think in terms of war.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php

### v. 15 — "The eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their cry."

God watches His people with approval and attentiveness; His ears catch their every cry. Spurgeon: "Their cry he hears at once, even as a mother is sure to hear her sick babe; the cry may be broken, plaintive, unhappy, feeble, unbelieving, yet the Father's quick ear catches each note."
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php

### v. 16 — "But the face of the LORD is against those who do evil, to wipe out all memory of them from the earth."

A sharp contrast: for the righteous, God's eyes and ears are attentive; for evildoers, His *face* is set *against* them. Gill: this is "not against everyone that sins… but against them that live in sin, whose course of life is a series of wickedness." The threat is utter destruction — their very remembrance cut off.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/34.htm , https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/

### v. 17 — "The righteous cry out, and the LORD hears; He delivers them from all their troubles."

The promise of v. 15 is now amplified. The righteous "cry out" — the Hebrew word suggests a cry under oppression. God delivers from *all* troubles: inward (corruption, Satan's assaults, desertion) and outward (affliction, loss, persecution). Gill notes the "righteous" is supplied in translation but is implied from the context.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/34.htm , https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/

### v. 18 — "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit."

This was a word of profound comfort to David's men at Adullam — those in debt, distress, and discontent. The brokenhearted are not objects of God's scorn but of His special nearness. Spurgeon: "Broken hearts think God is far away, when he is really most near to them; their eyes are holden so that they see not their best friend." Clarke explains "contrite" as "the beaten-out spirit" — the hammer is implied, breaking the ore and plating out the metal. Meyer: "A bird with a broken wing, an animal with a broken leg, a woman with a broken heart, a man with a broken purpose in life… God draws nigh."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php

### v. 19 — "Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him from them all."

The psalm does not promise a trouble-free life. "Many are the afflictions" — David knew this from experience (hunted by Saul, fleeing among enemies, hiding in caves). Spurgeon: "Scripture does not flatter us like the story books with the idea that goodness will secure us from trouble." But the "blessed *but*" follows: God delivers from them *all*. Maclaren: "'Many are the afflictions,' but more are the deliverances."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php

**On prosperity teaching:** The sites reviewed (Enduring Word, Spurgeon, Gill, Precept Austin) do not teach a "prosperity gospel" reading of this psalm. They consistently note that the promises of deliverance and provision are real but must be understood in light of God's sovereign wisdom — sometimes "wants and crosses are more needful" than abundance (Poole). The "good thing" promised in v. 10 is what God deems good, not necessarily what we desire. Spurgeon on v. 19 explicitly says goodness does *not* secure us from trouble.

### v. 20 — "He protects all his bones; not one of them will be broken."

David could look at his own body: despite many battles, not a single bone had been broken. Yet Spurgeon notes that since good people *have* suffered broken bones, this must also carry a spiritual meaning — no fatal injury to the soul, no essential part of the believer's being broken. Most importantly, John 19:36 applies this verse to Christ on the cross: the Roman soldiers did not break Jesus' legs because He was already dead, fulfilling this Scripture. David spoke beyond his own experience, prophetically pointing to the Messiah.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php

### v. 21 — "Evil will slay the wicked, and the haters of the righteous will be condemned."

The wicked are destroyed by their own evil. Poole offers two interpretations: (1) "The evil of sin. His own wickedness, though designed against others, shall destroy himself." Or (2) "The evil of misery" — the afflictions that refine the righteous will destroy the wicked. Spurgeon: "Ungodly men only need rope enough and they will hang themselves; their own iniquities shall be their punishment."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php

### v. 22 — "The LORD redeems His servants, and none who take refuge in Him will be condemned."

The psalm closes with redemption and security. "Redeems" implies purchase with price and power. Even under the Old Covenant, David knew freedom from condemnation — a truth Paul would later elaborate in Romans 8:1 ("no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus"). "None who take refuge in Him will be condemned" (or "desolate," as some translations render it). Spurgeon: "Believer, thou shalt never be deserted, forsaken, given up to ruin. God, even thy God, is thy guardian and friend, and bliss is thine."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/ , https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps034.php

## Tradition-Specific Distinctives (What Could Be Found)

### Reformed / Baptist on v. 7
The strongest tradition-specific difference noted is on **v. 7 (the angel of the LORD)**. Reformed Baptists like Gill and Spurgeon interpret the angel as the pre-incarnate Christ; Calvin (Reformed) takes it collectively as the angelic host. Lutherans (Keil & Delitzsch) side with the Christological reading. See detailed notes at v. 7 above.

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
The Enduring Word commentary (David Guzik, often used in charismatic circles) highlights the experiential dimension: v. 8 ("taste and see") as a *spiritual sense* where "faith is like tasting or seeing, and the experience itself becomes the proof." The angelic encampment of v. 7 is taken as support for belief in guardian angels. No prosperity-gospel interpretation was found in the sources; Guzik consistently notes that the promises must be understood within God's sovereign purposes.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-34/

### Methodist / Wesleyan Holiness
No specifically Wesleyan material on Psalm 34 was retrieved from seedbed.com or wesley.nnu.edu within the search limits.

### Lutheran
Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran scholars) take "the angel of the LORD" in v. 7 as the pre-incarnate Mediator, not a collective of angelic beings. The Vulgate's rendering (*immittet angelus Dominus*) and the LXX's use of παρεμβαλεῖ are discussed at length. No material from lcms.org or 1517.org was retrieved within limits.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/34-7.html

### Catholic and Orthodox
**Could not be accessed.** No results from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org were retrieved within the search and fetch limits.

### Modern Scholarship
Ellicott's commentary (accessed in excerpt form) argues the psalm is of late, possibly post-exilic origin, with the Davidic superscription being "of no historic value" — a reading from wordplay rather than genuine historical memory. The Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges similarly notes "thought and style are those of the Book of Proverbs, and apparently of a later age." The NET Bible notes (cited at Precept Austin) observe that the name "Abimelech" instead of "Achish" suggests the tradition may be "confused on this point," though "Abimelech" was possibly a royal title. No material from bibleodyssey.org was retrieved.
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/34.htm , https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-34-commentary
